chapters.n: After the wars and conflicts described in Words of Mormon, King Benjamin enjoys peace for the rest of his life. Mormon’s abridgment of the large plates resumes here.
Benjamin had three sons—Mosiah, Helorum, and Helaman. He made sure they learned their ancestors’ language and prophecies so they would understand God’s dealings.

f.g: Not the same as the later Helaman, son of Alma.

chapters.n: He taught them that without the brass plates, they would be living in spiritual ignorance, unaware of God’s mysteries.

f.g: Truths about God known only by revelation.

chapters.n: Lehi could not have remembered everything without the plates. He had been taught the Egyptian language, so he could read them and teach his children, who taught theirs.
Without these God-preserved records, even their ancestors would have lost faith, like the Lamanites, whose incorrect traditions kept them from the truth.
Benjamin testifies the brass plates and the plates of Nephi are true; they can be sure because the records are right before them.
He urges his sons to search the records diligently and keep the commandments so they will prosper, as God promised.
Benjamin taught his sons much more than is recorded here.
Growing old and nearing death, Benjamin decides to hand the kingdom to one of his sons.

f.w: go the way of all the earth

chapters.n: He tells Mosiah to proclaim a gathering of everyone—both the people of Zarahemla and the people of Mosiah—so he can announce Mosiah as king. Many scholars note parallels to ancient Israelite coronation and covenant festivals.
Benjamin will give the people a name to distinguish them, because they have diligently kept God’s commandments.

f.w: I shall give this people a name

chapters.n: This name can never be erased except by their own sin.
If this favored people turn wicked and unfaithful, God will withdraw his protection and they will become as weak as the Lamanites.

f.g: Unfaithful to God’s covenant, as well as morally unfaithful.

chapters.n: Without God’s protection, their ancestors would have fallen to the Lamanites long ago.
Benjamin then gives Mosiah charge of the kingdom’s affairs.
He also entrusts Mosiah with the sacred objects: the brass plates, the plates of Nephi, the sword of Laban, and the Liahona—the ball that guided Lehi according to their faith.
When Lehi’s family was unfaithful, the Liahona stopped working; they faltered and suffered hunger and hardship to remind them of their duty.
Mosiah obeys, summoning everyone in Zarahemla to come to the temple to hear his father.
Responding to Mosiah’s proclamation, people from all over the land travel to the temple to hear King Benjamin.
So many came that they couldn’t be counted—a sign of how the people had grown in peace.
They brought the firstborn of their flocks to offer sacrifices under the law of Moses, which pointed toward Christ.
They came to thank God for bringing them from Jerusalem, protecting them, and giving them just teachers and a just king—so they could be filled with love for God and others.

f.w: filled with love towards God and all men

chapters.n: Families camped around the temple, each in its own tent—parents, children, and grandchildren together.

f.g: Many scholars compare this to Israel’s Feast of Tabernacles, when families lived in booths (Leviticus 23:34-43).

chapters.n: Every tent faced the temple so families could stay inside and still hear the king. Many find this a lovely image: a home oriented toward the temple.

f.g: A symbol of families turned toward God.

chapters.n: The crowd was too large for the temple, so Benjamin had a tower built to speak from.
Even so, not everyone could hear, so his words were written down and circulated. This is one reason we have the sermon today.
Benjamin begins: he didn’t call them here to take his words lightly, but to listen with ears, hearts, and minds so God’s mysteries could be opened to them.
He doesn’t want them to fear him or think he is more than mortal. A humble king.
He is just like them, with physical and mental weaknesses, yet chosen by the people, consecrated by his father, and preserved by God to serve them with all his strength.
He has spent his days serving them and never sought their wealth.
He never imprisoned people unjustly, allowed slavery, murder, plunder, theft, or adultery, but taught them God’s commandments.
He even worked with his own hands so they wouldn’t carry heavy taxes. They themselves can vouch for this—a sharp contrast to later King Noah.
He isn’t boasting or accusing—just showing he can face God with a clear conscience.
Serving them was really serving God, so there is nothing to boast about.
A famous line: when you serve other people, you are serving God.

f.w: ye are only in the service of your God

chapters.n: If the king serves them, shouldn’t they serve one another?

f.w: ought not ye to labor to serve one another

chapters.n: If they feel he deserves thanks, how much more should they thank their heavenly King!
Even if they gave God all the thanks their souls could hold—for creating them, preserving them, giving joy and peace…
…and served him with all their hearts—he who gives them breath moment by moment—they would still be “unprofitable servants,” never able to repay him.
All God asks is obedience. He promised that the obedient will prosper, and he never changes his word.
First, he created you and gave you life, so you owe him.
Second, when you obey, he blesses you immediately—paying you again. So you are forever in his debt. What is there to boast about?

f.w: of what have ye to boast

chapters.n: Can we claim anything by ourselves? No—not even equal to the dust, for the dust we’re made from belongs to God.
Benjamin includes himself: he is no better than anyone, also made of dust, old and soon to return his body to the earth.

f.g: The body returns to the ground from which it came (Genesis 3:19).

chapters.n: He gathered them to be blameless before God, so their sins wouldn’t be on his head at judgment.

f.w: your blood should not come upon me

chapters.n: He wants to “rid his garments” of their blood before he dies, so his spirit can join the heavenly choirs praising God.
He announces he can no longer be their teacher or king.
His body trembles as he speaks, but God sustains him. He declares Mosiah king.
Keep doing what you’ve done: obey God’s commandments given through Mosiah, and you will prosper and be safe from enemies.
Beware of contention and of following the evil spirit his father Mosiah warned about.
Woe to anyone who chooses to follow that spirit and dies unrepentant—they “drink damnation” to their own soul by sinning against what they knew.
Everyone except little children knows they are eternally indebted to God and has been taught the prophets’ records.
Their ancestors spoke what the Lord commanded, so their words are just and true.
Knowing all this, if they rebel, they withdraw from the Spirit that would guide, bless, and preserve them.
Such a person is in open rebellion against God, an enemy to righteousness. The Lord can’t dwell in “unholy temples”—our bodies and lives must be clean for his Spirit.
If he dies unrepentant, justice awakens his soul to a vivid awareness of guilt, making him shrink from God’s presence in anguish like unquenchable fire.

f.w: lively sense of his own guilt
shrink from the presence of the Lord

chapters.n: Mercy has no claim on one who refuses to repent; he faces never-ending torment.
Benjamin addresses old, young, and children who can understand: wake up to the terrible situation of those who sin.

Now consider the opposite: the happy state of those who keep God’s commandments—blessed temporally and spiritually, and if faithful to the end, living with God in endless happiness. “O remember, remember.”
Benjamin continues: he has more to say, now about the future.
An angel from God had awakened Benjamin and stood before him to deliver this message.
The angel brings “glad tidings of great joy”—the same words angels later used announcing Jesus’ birth to the shepherds.
The Lord heard Benjamin’s prayers, saw his righteousness, and sent the angel so Benjamin and his people could rejoice.

Soon the “Lord Omnipotent,” the eternal God, will come down to live in a mortal body and perform mighty miracles—healing the sick, raising the dead, restoring sight and hearing. Jehovah himself would become mortal as Jesus.

f.g: The all-powerful Lord; here Jehovah, the premortal Christ.

chapters.n: He will cast out devils and evil spirits.

He will suffer temptation, pain, hunger, thirst, and fatigue beyond what any mortal could survive; blood will come from every pore because of the anguish of his people’s sins—a prophecy of Gethsemane.
His name will be Jesus Christ, Son of God, Creator of all—and his mother will be Mary. Remarkably specific prophecy over 120 years before his birth.

f.w: his mother shall be called Mary
the Father of heaven and earth
f.g: Father here in the sense of Creator (Ether 4:7; Mosiah 15:4).

chapters.n: He comes to his own people to bring salvation through faith, yet they will call him merely a man, say he has a devil, scourge, and crucify him.

f.w: say that he hath a devil

chapters.n: He will rise from the dead on the third day and will judge the world righteously.
His blood atones for those who died without knowing God’s will and for those who sinned in ignorance.
But woe to those who knowingly rebel; they can be saved only by repentance and faith in Christ.
God sent prophets to every people so that believers could be forgiven and rejoice as though Christ had already come.

f.w: as though he had already come

chapters.n: Because Israel was stubborn, God gave them the law of Moses.
God gave many signs, “types and shadows” pointing to Christ, but people hardened their hearts and missed that the law was worthless without Christ’s atoning blood.

f.g: Symbols and foreshadowings that point to something greater (Hebrews 10:1).

chapters.n: Little children are blessed. Whatever they inherit from Adam’s fall, Christ’s blood covers it. Latter-day Saints teach that little children need no baptism and are saved in Christ.

f.w: the blood of Christ atoneth for their sins

chapters.n: There is no other name, way, or means of salvation but through Christ.
Christ judges justly. Infants who die are safe, but adults bring condemnation on themselves unless they humble themselves like little children and trust in Christ’s atoning blood.

A key verse: the “natural man”—our fallen, selfish side—is an enemy to God unless we yield to the Holy Spirit and, through Christ’s Atonement, become a saint: childlike, meek, humble, patient, and loving.

f.g: The Spirit’s gentle invitations and promptings.
A holy person; a member of God’s covenant people.

chapters.n: Eventually the knowledge of the Savior will spread to every nation.

f.w: every nation, kindred, tongue, and people

chapters.n: Then no one but little children will be blameless, except through repentance and faith in Christ.
Even now, once Benjamin teaches his people, they too are accountable and can be blameless only through these teachings.
The angel says he has spoken what the Lord commanded.
These words will stand as a witness at judgment, when everyone is judged by their works.

f.w: judged, every man according to his works

chapters.n: The wicked will see their own guilt clearly and shrink from God’s presence in endless misery.

f.w: awful view of their own guilt

chapters.n: They drink from the cup of God’s wrath; justice can no more be denied than Adam’s fall could, so mercy has no more claim on them.

f.w: cup of the wrath of God

chapters.n: Their torment is like a lake of fire and brimstone that never goes out. The angel’s message closes with “Amen.”
As Benjamin finishes the angel’s words, he sees the whole crowd fallen to the ground, overcome by reverent awe of the Lord.

f.g: Reverent awe and respect for God.

chapters.n: Seeing their fallen state clearly, they cry with one voice for mercy, asking that Christ’s atoning blood be applied to them, and confessing faith in Jesus Christ.

f.w: apply the atoning blood of Christ

chapters.n: The Spirit came upon them. Filled with joy and peace of conscience, they received forgiveness through faith in Christ.
Benjamin speaks again, warmly calling them friends, brothers, kindred, and people.
If God’s goodness has awakened them to their own nothingness and fallen state…

f.g: Not worthlessness to God, but complete dependence on him.

chapters.n: …and if they know God’s power, wisdom, and patience, and the Atonement prepared from the foundation of the world for those who trust him and endure in faith to the end…
…then that person receives salvation through the Atonement prepared for all people of all times.
This is the only way to salvation; there are no other conditions.
Believe in God: that he exists, created all things, has all wisdom and power, and understands far more than we can.
Believe you must repent, forsake sin, humble yourselves, and sincerely ask forgiveness. And if you believe these things, do them.
Always remember God’s greatness and your own nothingness, his goodness and patience. Stay humble, pray daily, and hold fast to faith in Christ.

f.w: calling on the name of the Lord daily

chapters.n: If you do this, you will always rejoice, be filled with God’s love, retain a remission of sins, and grow in knowledge of truth. Forgiveness is kept alive through continued humility.

f.w: retain a remission of your sins

chapters.n: You won’t want to hurt others but will live peacefully and treat people fairly. Conversion changes behavior.

f.w: render to every man according to that which is his due

chapters.n: You won’t let your children go hungry or naked, nor let them break God’s laws, fight, and serve the devil.

f.g: The devil, author and ruler of sin.

chapters.n: Instead, you will teach them truth, seriousness, and to love and serve one another.

f.w: teach them to love one another

chapters.n: You will help those in need, share your goods, and never turn away a beggar to perish.
Perhaps you’ll think, “He brought his poverty on himself; I won’t help—he deserves it.”
Anyone who thinks that must repent, or they lose their place in God’s kingdom.
A famous question: “Are we not all beggars?” Everything we have—food, clothing, wealth—comes from God.
Just now they begged God for forgiveness. Did he turn them away? No—he poured out his Spirit and filled them with joy beyond words.

f.g: Could not speak, so great was their joy.

chapters.n: If God gives you what you rightly ask in faith, how much more should you share with each other.
If you condemn a beggar, your own condemnation is even more deserved, since you withhold goods that belong to God—and you never even ask forgiveness.

f.w: doth not belong to you but to God

chapters.n: Woe to such a person—his wealth will perish with him. This is aimed at the rich.

f.w: his substance shall perish with him

chapters.n: To the poor who have just enough to get by: if you can’t give, say in your heart, “I give not because I have not, but if I had I would give.”
If you mean that sincerely, you are guiltless. If not, you’re condemned for coveting what you don’t have. God judges the heart.

f.g: Wrongfully desire what belongs to another.

chapters.n: To retain a remission of your sins day by day, share with the poor according to what you have—feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit and relieve the sick, spiritually and temporally.

f.w: feeding the hungry, clothing the naked

chapters.n: Do this wisely and in order. You don’t have to run faster than you have strength—but be diligent to win the prize. A balanced, often-quoted counsel.

f.w: run faster than he has strength

chapters.n: Return what you borrow as agreed; otherwise you sin and may lead your neighbor to sin too, perhaps through anger.

f.w: return the thing that he borroweth

chapters.n: Benjamin can’t list every possible sin—there are too many ways.
But this he can say: watch your thoughts, words, and deeds, keep the commandments, and stay faithful to the end, or you will perish. “Remember, and perish not.”

f.w: watch yourselves, and your thoughts, and your words, and your deeds

chapters.n: Benjamin sends messengers among the crowd to ask whether they believe what he taught.
With one voice they answer yes—and they know it is true, because the Spirit has worked a “mighty change” in their hearts. They no longer want to do evil, only good.

f.w: no more disposition to do evil
f.g: No longer inclined or wanting to sin.

chapters.n: Through God’s goodness and his Spirit they glimpse the future so clearly that, if it were appropriate, they could prophesy.
Their faith in the king’s words brought this knowledge and great joy.
They are ready to covenant with God to do his will and obey him all their lives, to avoid the torment the angel described.

f.w: cup of the wrath of God

chapters.n: Benjamin rejoices: this is exactly what he hoped to hear, and their covenant is righteous.
Because of their covenant, they are now called the children of Christ—his sons and daughters, spiritually born of him that day through their changed hearts.
Under Christ as their “head,” they are made free; there is no other. So Benjamin invites them to take upon themselves the name of Christ.

f.w: take upon you the name of Christ

f.g: Leader, authority—as the head of a family or covenant.

chapters.n: Those who do this will stand at God’s right hand—the place of favor—and will be known by Christ’s name.
Those who don’t take Christ’s name will be called by another name and stand on God’s left hand.
This is the name Benjamin promised that could never be erased—except by transgression. So guard against sin.
Keep the name written in your hearts always, so you can recognize the voice and the name by which Christ will call you.
How can anyone know a master he never served—a stranger far from his thoughts? We come to know Christ by serving him.

f.w: how knoweth a man the master whom he has not served

chapters.n: A homely example: no one keeps a neighbor’s donkey among his flocks—he drives it away. Likewise, Christ won’t claim those who don’t bear his name.
Be steadfast and immovable, always rich in good works, so Christ can “seal you his” and bring you to eternal life. Benjamin’s sermon ends here.
Benjamin recorded the names of everyone who covenanted to keep God’s commandments—an early example of keeping records of covenant members.
Every person old enough—everyone except little children—made the covenant and took Christ’s name.
Benjamin consecrated Mosiah king, gave him charge of the kingdom, and appointed priests to teach and remind people of their oath. Then everyone went home with their families.

f.g: A solemn promise to God—here their covenant.

chapters.n: Mosiah began reigning at age thirty, about 476 years after Lehi left Jerusalem (around 124 BC).
Benjamin lived three more years and then died.
King Mosiah followed the Lord faithfully, keeping his laws and commandments.
Mosiah had his people farm, and he farmed too, so he wouldn’t burden them, just as his father had. There was peace for three years.
After three years of peace, Mosiah wanted to learn what happened to the group that had gone back to the land of Lehi-Nephi. His people kept pestering him about it, having heard nothing for years.

f.g: The Nephites’ original homeland, which they had left under Mosiah I.

chapters.n: Mosiah allowed sixteen strong men to go and find them.
Their leader was Ammon, a strong descendant of Zarahemla—not the same as the later missionary Ammon, son of Mosiah.

f.g: A different man from Ammon the son of Mosiah (Alma 17).

chapters.n: They didn’t know the way, so they wandered in the wilderness forty days.

f.g: A number often linked in scripture with testing and preparation.

chapters.n: After forty days they camped on a hill north of the land of Shilom.
Ammon took three companions—Amaleki, Helem, and Hem—and went down into the land of Nephi.
They met the king outside the city, were surrounded by guards, tied up, and put in prison.
After two days they were brought before the king, untied, and ordered to answer his questions.
The king introduces himself: Limhi, son of Noah, grandson of Zeniff, who led a group from Zarahemla to reclaim their ancestors’ land.
Limhi asks why they boldly approached the city walls while he was outside the gate with his guards.
He spared them only to question them; otherwise his guards would have killed them.
Ammon bows respectfully, thanks God he is still alive, and promises to speak boldly.
If Limhi had known who he was, he wouldn’t have bound him. Ammon explains he is from Zarahemla, searching for Zeniff’s people.
Limhi is overjoyed—their relatives in Zarahemla are still alive! He plans a day of rejoicing.
Limhi’s people are in bondage to the Lamanites under crushing taxes. He would rather be slaves to the Nephites than keep paying tribute to the Lamanite king.

f.g: Forced payment from a conquered people.

chapters.n: Limhi frees Ammon’s men and sends for the rest of the group so they can eat, drink, and rest after their hard journey.
The next day Limhi summons his people to the temple to hear him.
He tells them to lift up their heads: deliverance is near. Their past struggles have failed, but one effective effort remains.
Trust in the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who freed Israel from Egypt, parted the Red Sea, and fed them manna. Limhi recalls the Exodus as a pattern for their own deliverance.

f.w: walk through the Red Sea on dry ground

chapters.n: The same God led their fathers from Jerusalem and preserved them. Their bondage came because of their sins.
Zeniff, too eager to reclaim the land, was tricked by King Laman, who gave him Lehi-Nephi and Shilom through a treaty.
Laman’s goal all along was to enslave them. Now they pay half of everything—grain, flocks, possessions—or lose their lives.

f.w: one half of all we have

chapters.n: Isn’t this burden heavy? Isn’t their suffering great? They have good reason to mourn.
Many have been killed for nothing, all because of sin.
If they had not sinned, the Lord wouldn’t have allowed this. But they ignored him, and contention led to bloodshed among themselves.
They even killed a prophet who warned them and foretold Christ’s coming—Abinadi, whose story appears in chapters 11–17.

f.w: a prophet of the Lord have they slain

chapters.n: Abinadi taught that Christ is God, the Father of all, who would take on a human body in the image in which man was first created, and come among people in flesh and blood.

f.w: Christ was the God, the Father of all things

chapters.n: For this they killed him and committed other sins. Is it any wonder they are in bondage?
Limhi quotes the Lord: I won’t help my people while they sin, but will block their way so they don’t prosper.
Sow filth and reap chaff in a whirlwind—and the effect is poison. Sin produces worthless, harmful results.

f.w: reap the chaff thereof in the whirlwind

f.g: The useless husks blown away when grain is threshed.

chapters.n: Sow filth and reap the “east wind,” bringing sudden destruction.

f.g: A scorching desert wind that withers crops; a biblical symbol of judgment.

chapters.n: The Lord’s warning has come true; they are suffering.
But if they turn to the Lord with all their hearts, trust him, and serve him diligently, he will deliver them in his own way and time.

f.w: according to his own will and pleasure

chapters.n: Mormon notes he recorded only part of Limhi’s speech. Limhi then told his people about their relatives in Zarahemla.
Limhi had Ammon stand and recount everything that had happened in Zarahemla since Zeniff left.
Ammon also shared and explained King Benjamin’s last sermon, so Limhi’s people learned of it too.

f.w: last words which king Benjamin had taught

chapters.n: Then Limhi dismissed the people to their homes.
Limhi showed Ammon the record of his people since they left Zarahemla—the record found in Mosiah 9–22.
After Ammon read it, Limhi asked whether he could interpret languages. Ammon could not.
Limhi explains he once sent 43 people into the wilderness to find Zarahemla and ask for help.
They got lost, missed Zarahemla, and found a land of many waters covered with bones and ruins—once home to a people as numerous as Israel. These were the Jaredites.

f.g: The great multitudes of ancient Israel.

chapters.n: As proof they brought back 24 gold plates covered with engravings.
They also brought large breastplates of brass and copper, still in perfect condition.
And swords whose hilts had rotted and whose blades had rusted. No one could read the plates, so Limhi asks Ammon again: can you translate?
Does Ammon know anyone who can? Limhi longs to know who these destroyed people were and why they perished.
Yes—Ammon knows a man who can translate ancient records using “interpreters,” a gift from God. Only those commanded may look in them; such a person is called a seer.

f.g: One who “sees” by divine gift—past, future, or hidden things.

chapters.n: That man is King Mosiah of Zarahemla.
Limhi says a seer is greater than a prophet.
Ammon agrees: a seer is also a revelator and prophet. No gift is greater short of having God’s own power. Latter-day Saints sustain their leaders as “prophets, seers, and revelators.”

f.w: a seer is a revelator and a prophet also

chapters.n: A seer can know the past and future; through seers, secret and hidden things come to light that couldn’t be known any other way.
So God provides a way for people, through faith, to work miracles and greatly bless others.
Limhi rejoices and thanks God, sure the plates hold great mysteries and the interpreters were prepared to reveal them.
He marvels at God’s works and patience—and at how closed people’s minds are, refusing to seek wisdom or let her guide them.

f.w: neither do they desire that she should rule over them
f.g: Wisdom is pictured as a woman, as in Proverbs 1:20-33.

chapters.n: People are like a wild flock running from the shepherd, scattering, and being devoured by wild beasts.

f.w: a wild flock which fleeth from the shepherd

chapters.n: The record now jumps back about 80 years and shifts to Zeniff’s own first-person account. He had once been sent to spy on the Lamanites but saw good among them and didn’t want them destroyed.

f.w: land of our fathers' first inheritance
f.g: The land of Nephi, where Nephi first settled after separating from Laman and Lemuel (2 Nephi 5:5-8).

chapters.n: Zeniff argued for a treaty; their harsh, bloodthirsty leader ordered him killed. A civil fight broke out, most of the army died, and the survivors returned to Zarahemla.
Still “over-zealous” to reclaim their ancestral land, Zeniff gathered another group. They suffered famine because they were slow to remember the Lord.
After much wandering, they camped where their brethren had been killed, near their ancestors’ land.
Zeniff and four men went into the city to meet the Lamanite king and see whether they could settle peacefully.
The king covenanted to let them possess the lands of Lehi-Nephi and Shilom.
He ordered his own people out, and Zeniff’s people moved in.
They began building and repairing the walls of Lehi-Nephi and Shilom.
They planted corn, wheat, barley, “neas,” and “sheum,” plus fruit, and began to prosper.

f.g: An untranslated word for some crop; its identity is unknown.
An untranslated word; some scholars link it to an ancient Akkadian word for a grain such as barley.

chapters.n: But King Laman’s generosity was a trick—he wanted to bring them into bondage.
After twelve years, Laman grew nervous that Zeniff’s people were getting too strong to conquer.
Zeniff describes the Lamanites as lazy idol-worshippers who wanted to live off the Nephites’ work and flocks.
So Laman stirred up his people, and war began.
In Zeniff’s thirteenth year, a large Lamanite army attacked his people south of Shilom as they tended flocks and fields, killing them and stealing livestock and crops.
Survivors fled to the city of Nephi and begged Zeniff for protection.
Zeniff armed his people with every weapon they could make—bows, swords, cimeters, clubs, slings—and led them into battle.
They went “in the strength of the Lord,” crying mightily to him, remembering how he had delivered their ancestors.

f.w: in the strength of the Lord

chapters.n: God answered. In a day and a night they killed 3,043 Lamanites and drove them out.
Zeniff personally helped bury the dead. With great sorrow, he notes 279 of his own people died. War’s cost is grief on both sides.
After the first war, Zeniff’s people reestablished their kingdom. Zeniff had every kind of weapon made in case the Lamanites returned.
He posted guards around the land so they wouldn’t be surprised again, protecting people and flocks.
They lived in their ancestral land for twenty-two years.
The men farmed all kinds of grain and fruit.
The women spun and wove fine linen and cloth. Everyone worked, and they enjoyed twenty-two years of peace.
King Laman died, and his son stirred the Lamanites to war against Zeniff’s people.
Zeniff had spies around the land of Shemlon to watch for Lamanite preparations.
The Lamanites came north of Shilom in large numbers, armed with bows, swords, cimeters, stones, and slings, heads shaved and wearing leather loincloths.
Zeniff hid the women and children in the wilderness and organized every man able to fight, old and young, into ranks by age.
Old as he was, Zeniff led his people into battle “in the strength of the Lord.”
The Lamanites knew nothing of the Lord and relied on their own considerable strength.
Zeniff explains the Lamanites’ inherited grievances: they believed they had been wronged—driven from Jerusalem by their fathers’ sins, mistreated in the wilderness and at sea.
They also felt wronged in the promised land, all because Nephi was more faithful and so the Lord favored him and made him leader.

f.w: he took the lead of their journey

chapters.n: Laman and Lemuel were angry because they didn’t understand God’s ways, and on the ship because they hardened their hearts.

f.w: wroth with him upon the waters

chapters.n: In the new land, they resented Nephi for supposedly taking power from them and tried to kill him.
When Nephi left as the Lord commanded, taking the brass plates, they claimed he had robbed them. A grudge was handed down for centuries.
They taught their children to hate, murder, and plunder the Nephites—an “eternal hatred.” Teaching grudges to children can poison generations.
Zeniff concludes that King Laman tricked him with false promises into bringing his people there to be destroyed.
Having explained this, Zeniff rallied his people to fight with all their might, trusting in the Lord.
They drove the Lamanites out with such great slaughter that they couldn’t count the dead.
Then they went home and resumed tending flocks and farming.
Old now, Zeniff gives the kingdom to one of his sons—Noah—and ends his record with a blessing on his people.
Zeniff made his son Noah king, but Noah did not follow his father’s righteous ways. Mormon’s narration resumes.
Noah followed his own desires, took many wives and concubines, and led his people into sexual sin and wickedness.
He taxed them one fifth of everything they owned—precious metals, “ziff,” livestock, and grain.

f.g: An untranslated word for some metal; its identity is unknown.

chapters.n: All of it supported Noah, his priests, and their wives and concubines. He changed how the kingdom was run—the opposite of Benjamin, who labored to avoid taxing his people.
He removed the priests his father had consecrated and appointed proud men in their place.
These priests lived lazily in idolatry and immorality, supported by the people’s heavy labor.
The people became idolaters too, deceived by the flattering words of the king and his priests.
Noah built many elegant, spacious buildings decorated with wood and precious metals.
He built himself a large palace with an ornate throne of fine wood, gold, silver, and precious things.
He had workmen decorate the temple inside with fine wood, copper, and brass.
The high priests’ seats were raised above the others, plated with gold, with a breastwork to lean on while they spoke lies. The furniture itself shows their pride.
Noah built a very high tower near the temple, from which he could see Shilom, Shemlon, and all the surrounding land.
He also built in Shilom and put a great tower on the hill north of Shilom, all funded by taxing his people.

f.w: hill north of the land Shilom

chapters.n: Noah set his heart on riches and lived in reckless pleasure with his wives and concubines; his priests spent time with prostitutes.
He planted vineyards and made lots of wine, becoming a drunkard along with his people.
The Lamanites began picking off small groups of Noah’s people in their fields and pastures.
Noah sent too few guards; the Lamanites killed them and drove off many flocks.
Noah’s armies pushed the Lamanites back for a while and returned celebrating the spoils.
This victory made them proud. They boasted that fifty of them could stand against thousands and delighted in bloodshed—because of their wicked leaders.
A man named Abinadi began prophesying: the Lord has seen their wickedness, and unless they repent, he will visit them in anger.

f.g: Nothing is recorded of his background; he appears suddenly, like Elijah.
The classic formula of a prophet delivering God’s message.

chapters.n: Unless they repent, they will be delivered to their enemies and brought into bondage.
Then they will know he is the Lord, a “jealous God” who holds his people accountable.
Without repentance they will be enslaved, and only the Almighty can free them.
When they cry for help, the Lord will be slow to hear them and will let enemies strike them.
Unless they repent in sackcloth and ashes and cry mightily, he will not hear or rescue them.

f.g: Rough clothing and ashes—ancient signs of mourning and repentance (Jonah 3:6).

chapters.n: The people were furious and tried to kill Abinadi, but the Lord delivered him.
Noah, angry too, asks scornfully, “Who is Abinadi… or who is the Lord?”—echoing Pharaoh’s defiance.
He orders Abinadi brought to him to be killed, accusing him of stirring up contention.
Blinded, the people hardened their hearts and kept trying to capture Abinadi. Noah refused to repent.
Two years later Abinadi returns in disguise. The Lord says the people have hardened their hearts and not repented, so his fierce anger will come.

f.g: Since the people had tried to kill him (Mosiah 11:26).

chapters.n: Woe to this generation: they will be enslaved, struck on the cheek, driven, killed, and left for vultures, dogs, and wild beasts.
Noah’s life will be valued like a garment in a hot furnace—quickly burned. This later came true when Noah died by fire.

f.w: a garment in a hot furnace

chapters.n: The Lord will send famine and plague; the people will howl in misery all day.
They will carry burdens strapped to their backs and be driven like a mute donkey—fulfilled under the Lamanites.

f.g: A donkey that cannot speak—an image of helpless forced labor.

chapters.n: Hail, the scorching east wind, and insects will destroy their crops.
A great plague will strike them—all because of their wickedness.
Unless they repent, they will be wiped out. Yet their record will be preserved for future nations, to reveal their sins as a warning.

f.w: they shall leave a record behind them

chapters.n: Angry, the people tied up Abinadi and brought him to the king, accusing him of prophesying destruction.
They report that he said the king’s life will be like a garment in a fire.
And that Noah would be like a dry stalk trampled by animals.
And like thistle down scattered by the wind. They claim Abinadi only “pretends” the Lord said it.

f.g: Seed fluff easily blown away—a picture of a short, insignificant life.

chapters.n: “What great evil have you done?” they flatter the king—refusing to see their own sins.
They insist they and the king are innocent and Abinadi is lying.
“We are strong; we won’t be enslaved; you’ll keep prospering.” Their pride blinds them.
They hand Abinadi over for the king to do with as he pleases.
Noah imprisons Abinadi and calls a council of his priests.
The priests ask to question him, and the king has him brought in.
They try to trip him up so they can accuse him, but he answers boldly and confounds them, to their astonishment.
One priest asks what a well-known scripture means.

He quotes Isaiah 52:7: how beautiful are the feet of the messenger bringing good news of peace and salvation, telling Zion, “Thy God reigneth.” Perhaps he hoped to trap Abinadi by implying a prophet should bring good news, not doom.
Watchmen lift up their voices and sing together; they will “see eye to eye” when the Lord restores Zion.

f.g: Prophets who watch over God’s people and warn of danger.

chapters.n: Ruined Jerusalem is invited to burst into joyful song, for the Lord has comforted and redeemed his people.
The Lord has bared his arm before all nations, and everyone will see God’s salvation. Abinadi answers this question in Mosiah 15.
Abinadi turns the question back: you claim to be priests and prophets, yet you ask me what this means?
Woe to you for twisting the Lord’s ways! If you understand, you haven’t taught it.

f.w: perverting the ways of the Lord

chapters.n: They haven’t set their hearts on understanding, so they aren’t wise. What do they teach?
They answer: the law of Moses.
Then why don’t you keep it? Why chase riches, commit adultery, and lead the people into sin? The hypocrisy is the problem.

f.w: why do ye not keep it

chapters.n: Abinadi says they know he speaks truth and should tremble before God.
They will be punished. And what do they really know of the law? Does salvation come by the law of Moses?
They answer yes, salvation comes by the law of Moses.
Abinadi replies: keeping God’s commandments is required, beginning with those given to Moses on Sinai.
He begins the Ten Commandments: “I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of Egypt.”

f.w: I am the Lord thy God

chapters.n: First commandment: no other gods before the Lord.
Second: make no carved idol or image—pointed, since Noah’s people had become idolaters.
Abinadi asks: have you kept these? Have you taught them? No and no.
Noah orders his priests to kill Abinadi, calling him mad.
The priests try to seize him, but he resists them.
“Touch me not”: God will strike them, because his message isn’t finished. God will protect him until his work is done.

f.g: A warning that he is under divine protection.

chapters.n: He must fulfill God’s command. They are angry because he tells the truth and call him mad for speaking God’s word.
No one dared touch him; the Spirit was on him, and his face shone brightly, like Moses’ face on Sinai.
He spoke with God’s power and authority.
Since they cannot kill him yet, he will finish. The truth about their sins cuts them to the heart.
His words fill them with amazement and anger.
Once he finishes, it doesn’t matter what happens to him, as long as he is saved.

f.w: it matters not whither I go

chapters.n: What they do to him will be a “type and shadow” of things to come—foreshadowing Noah’s own death by fire and the later burning of believers.
He will read the rest of the commandments, because they aren’t written in their hearts.
He repeats the second commandment against carved images of anything in heaven, earth, or water.
Don’t bow down to idols. God is “jealous”—devoted to his covenant people—and the effects of hating him ripple through generations.

f.g: Hebrew qanna: zealous, demanding exclusive loyalty, as in a marriage covenant.

chapters.n: But he shows mercy to thousands who love him and keep his commandments—mercy far outweighs punishment.
Third: don’t take the Lord’s name in vain—using it lightly, falsely, or emptily.
Fourth: remember the Sabbath and keep it holy.
Work six days.
On the seventh, no one in the household works—not children, servants, animals, or visitors. Rest is for everyone.

f.w: stranger that is within thy gates

chapters.n: God made everything in six days and rested on the seventh, so he blessed and made it holy.
Fifth: honor your father and mother, with the promise of long life in the land.

f.w: Honor thy father and thy mother

chapters.n: Sixth: do not kill—murder. Ironically spoken to men about to kill a prophet.
Seventh and eighth: do not commit adultery; do not steal—both direct rebukes of Noah’s court, which lived in immorality on taxes.
Ninth: don’t lie about your neighbor—as the priests were doing about Abinadi.
Tenth: don’t covet anything that belongs to your neighbor. This commandment reaches the heart’s desires.
Have you taught the people to keep all these?
No—if they had, the Lord wouldn’t have needed to send Abinadi.
They said salvation comes by the law of Moses. Abinadi says they should still keep it for now, but a time will come when it won’t be needed—after Christ fulfills it.

f.w: no more be expedient to keep the law of Moses

chapters.n: Salvation does not come by the law alone. Without the Atonement God himself will make, everyone would perish despite the law.

f.w: atonement, which God himself shall make

chapters.n: Israel needed a very strict law because they were stubborn, quick to sin, and slow to remember God.

f.w: quick to do iniquity, and slow to remember

chapters.n: So God gave a law of daily rituals and ordinances to keep them remembering God and their duty.
All of these were “types”—symbols pointing to things to come, especially Christ.
Many didn’t understand the law because of hard hearts; they didn’t realize no one can be saved except through God’s redemption.
Moses and all the prophets since the world began prophesied of the Messiah and God’s redemption.
They foretold God himself coming down, taking human form, and going forth in mighty power.

f.w: take upon him the form of man

chapters.n: They also foretold he would bring about the resurrection and be oppressed and afflicted himself—leading into Isaiah 53 in the next chapter.
Abinadi now quotes Isaiah 53, the great prophecy of the suffering Messiah, to show the priests that the prophets foretold Christ. Who will believe this message about how God’s power is revealed?

f.g: God’s power to save, here embodied in the Messiah.

chapters.n: The Messiah will grow up like a fragile shoot from dry ground—humble, ordinary in appearance, with no outward glamour to attract people.
He will be despised and rejected, “a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.” People will turn away from him and think nothing of him.
He carries our griefs and sorrows, yet people assume he is being punished by God for his own faults. Mosiah reads “has borne” where the KJV has “hath borne.”

f.g: Thought to be struck down by God as a sinner.

chapters.n: He was wounded for our sins and bruised for our wrongdoing. The punishment that brings us peace fell on him, and his wounds heal us—the heart of the Atonement.

f.w: with his stripes we are healed

chapters.n: Like sheep we have all wandered off our own way, and the Lord placed all our sins on him.
Oppressed and afflicted, he stays silent, like a lamb led to slaughter or a sheep before shearers. Jesus was silent before his accusers.
Taken by unjust arrest and trial, he is cut off from the living for his people’s sins. “Who shall declare his generation?”—who will speak of his descendants? Abinadi answers in Mosiah 15:10-13.
He is assigned a grave among the wicked and with the rich in death, though he did no wrong and spoke no deceit. Jesus died between criminals and was buried in a rich man’s tomb.

f.w: with the rich in his death
made his grave with the wicked

chapters.n: It was the Lord’s will that he suffer. When his soul becomes an offering for sin, he will “see his seed” and his days will be prolonged—pointing to resurrection—and God’s purpose will succeed through him.
Seeing the results of his soul’s anguish, he will be satisfied. God’s righteous servant will justify many by bearing their sins.

f.g: Declare righteous; make right with God.

chapters.n: So God will give him a share with the great, because he poured out his life to death, was counted among sinners, carried many people’s sins, and pleaded for transgressors.
Abinadi’s central point: God himself—Jehovah, the premortal Christ—will come down among humanity and redeem his people.
Because he will live in a mortal body, he will be called the Son of God. By submitting his flesh to the Father’s will, he is both “the Father and the Son.”

f.w: subjected the flesh to the will of the Father

chapters.n: Father because he was conceived by God’s power (and fully carries the Father’s divine nature and will); Son because of his mortal flesh. Latter-day Saints understand this as describing Christ’s roles, not merging the Father and Son into one person.

f.w: The Father, because he was conceived by the power of God
f.g: Christ is called Father in roles such as Creator and through divine investiture of the Father’s authority.

chapters.n: They are “one God,” the Eternal Father of heaven and earth—Christ as Creator of all things.

f.w: Father of heaven and of earth

chapters.n: With his flesh subject to the Spirit, he will be tempted but not yield, and will allow himself to be mocked, whipped, rejected, and disowned.
After many miracles, he will be led away silent, like a sheep before the shearer—just as Isaiah said.

f.w: as a sheep before the shearer is dumb

chapters.n: He will be crucified and killed, his will “swallowed up” in the Father’s will—perfect submission, even to death.

f.w: swallowed up in the will of the Father

chapters.n: So God breaks the bonds of death and wins the victory, giving the Son power to intercede for humanity.
Ascended into heaven and full of compassion, he stands between us and justice, having taken on our sins and satisfied justice’s demands.

f.g: Deep, heartfelt mercy—“bowels” was the seat of emotion in older English.

chapters.n: Abinadi now answers Isaiah’s question: “Who shall declare his generation?” Who are the “seed” the Messiah will see after his offering for sin?
His seed are all who heard the prophets, believed the Lord would redeem them, and looked forward to forgiveness—the heirs of God’s kingdom.

f.w: heirs of the kingdom of God

chapters.n: They are those whose sins he bore and for whom he died. Are they not his children?
All the faithful prophets since the world began are also his seed.
These prophets published peace and salvation and told Zion, “Thy God reigneth!”—now Abinadi interprets the very verse the priest asked about.
How beautiful were the feet of past prophets!
How beautiful are the feet of those still proclaiming peace!
And how beautiful the feet of those who will proclaim peace forever after!
Most of all, how beautiful the feet of the Lord himself, “the founder of peace,” who redeemed his people.

f.g: The source and author of peace—Christ.

chapters.n: Without the redemption prepared from the foundation of the world, all humanity would have perished.
The bands of death will be broken; the Son reigns and has power over the dead, bringing resurrection.

f.w: bands of death shall be broken

chapters.n: There will be a first resurrection, beginning with Christ’s own, including the righteous from earlier times up to then.
The prophets and all who believed and kept God’s commandments will come forth in the first resurrection.
They will live with God, who redeemed them—eternal life through Christ.
Also included: those who died before Christ in ignorance, never hearing the gospel. Latter-day Saints connect this with the gospel being taught to the dead.

f.w: not having salvation declared unto them

chapters.n: Little children also have eternal life.

f.w: little children also have eternal life

chapters.n: But tremble: the Lord does not redeem those who willfully rebel, knowing his commandments and refusing to keep them, and die in their sins.
Salvation does not come to them. The Lord can’t deny himself or deny justice when it has a rightful claim.
The time will come when the Lord’s salvation is declared to every nation and people.

f.w: every nation, kindred, tongue, and people

chapters.n: Abinadi now quotes the rest of the Isaiah passage: watchmen will sing together and see eye to eye when the Lord brings again Zion.
Ruined Jerusalem will burst into joyful song, for the Lord has comforted and redeemed it.
The Lord will show his power before all nations, and the whole earth will see God’s salvation.
Abinadi stretches out his hand and declares that one day every nation will see the Lord’s salvation and confess that his judgments are fair.

f.w: confess before God that his judgments are just

chapters.n: Then the wicked will be cast out, weeping and gnashing their teeth, because they refused to listen to the Lord.

f.g: Grind teeth in anguish or rage.

chapters.n: They are carnal and devilish, under the devil’s power—the “old serpent” who deceived Adam and Eve. Through the Fall, humanity became carnal, sensual, and devilish, knowing good and evil.
So all humanity was lost and would have stayed lost forever if God had not redeemed them.
But anyone who clings to their carnal nature and keeps rebelling stays fallen, as if there had been no redemption at all. Christ’s rescue must be accepted.

f.w: as though there was no redemption made

chapters.n: Speaking of future events as already done, Abinadi says that without Christ coming into the world, there could be no redemption.

f.w: as though they had already come

chapters.n: Without Christ’s resurrection breaking death’s bonds, there would be no resurrection for anyone.
But there is a resurrection! The grave has no victory; death’s sting is swallowed up in Christ.
Christ is the light and life of the world—light that never darkens, life that never ends.

f.w: light and the life of the world

chapters.n: Our mortal, decaying bodies will become immortal and incorruptible, and all will stand before God to be judged by their works.

f.w: this corruption shall put on incorruption

chapters.n: The good rise to endless life and happiness; the evil to endless damnation, handed over to the devil who controlled them.
They followed their own carnal desires and never called on the Lord while his arms of mercy were open. Warned and commanded to repent, they refused.
Shouldn’t you tremble and repent, remembering that only through Christ can you be saved?
If you teach the law of Moses, teach that it is a shadow of things to come—a symbol of Christ.

f.w: a shadow of those things which are to come

chapters.n: Teach that redemption comes through Christ the Lord, “the very Eternal Father.” Abinadi’s great sermon ends with “Amen.”
When Abinadi finished, King Noah ordered his priests to have him put to death.
But one priest—Alma, a young descendant of Nephi—believed Abinadi, knowing his accusations were true, and pleaded with the king to let him go in peace. One listener changes Nephite history.

f.g: Alma the Elder, founder of the church among the Nephites and father of Alma the Younger.

chapters.n: Noah was furious, expelled Alma, and sent servants to kill him.
Alma fled and hid for many days, writing down all of Abinadi’s words. Thanks to him, we have the sermon.
Guards surrounded Abinadi, bound him, and imprisoned him.
After three days of consulting with his priests, Noah brought him back.
Noah announces they have found grounds to sentence him to death.
The charge: saying God himself would come down among people. Abinadi will die unless he takes back what he said—a charge resembling the blasphemy accusation against Jesus.
Abinadi refuses: his words are true. He allowed himself to be captured so they would know it.
He will suffer even to death and not retract. If they kill him, they shed innocent blood, which will testify against them at judgment.
Noah, afraid of God’s judgments, was about to release him.
But the priests accused Abinadi of insulting the king, inflaming Noah’s anger, so he handed him over to be killed—a pattern like Pilate yielding to pressure.
They bound him and burned him with flaming bundles of sticks until he died.

f.g: Bundles of sticks used as fuel.

chapters.n: As the flames began to burn him, he cried out to them.
Their descendants will cause many believers to suffer death by fire, just as he does—fulfilled when the priests’ descendants burned believers.
They will suffer every kind of disease because of their sins.
They will be struck on every side and scattered like a flock chased by wild beasts.
They will be hunted, captured, and suffer death by fire—fulfilled for Noah himself and later for his priests’ followers.
God brings vengeance on those who destroy his people. Abinadi’s last words: “O God, receive my soul”—echoing Stephen and Jesus.
Abinadi died by fire, refusing to deny God’s commandments, sealing his testimony with his life. He is the first named martyr in the Book of Mormon’s record.

f.w: sealed the truth of his words by his death

chapters.n: Alma repented of his sins and secretly began teaching Abinadi’s words among the people. Conversion starts with personal repentance.
He taught about the future, the resurrection, and redemption through Christ’s power, suffering, death, resurrection, and ascension.
He taught privately to avoid the king, and many believed.
Believers gathered at a place called Mormon, on the land’s border, named by the king and sometimes overrun by wild animals.

f.g: The place-name that the later prophet Mormon would carry (3 Nephi 5:12).

chapters.n: There was a spring of pure water and a thicket of small trees where Alma hid by day from the king’s searches.
Everyone who believed went there to hear him.
Over many days a good number gathered, and Alma taught repentance, redemption, and faith in the Lord.
At the waters of Mormon, Alma asks if they want to enter God’s fold and be his people—willing to bear one another’s burdens so they are lighter.

f.g: God’s flock; his church and people.

chapters.n: Willing to mourn with those who mourn, comfort those needing comfort, and stand as witnesses of God at all times and places, so they may be redeemed and have eternal life. This describes the baptismal covenant.
If so, why not be baptized as a witness of your covenant to serve God and keep his commandments, so he can pour out his Spirit more abundantly?

f.w: pour out his Spirit more abundantly

chapters.n: The people clapped for joy: “This is the desire of our hearts.”
Alma took Helam into the water and prayed that the Lord would pour out his Spirit so he could do this work with a holy heart.

f.g: The first person baptized; a city was later named after him (Mosiah 23:19-20).

chapters.n: Filled with the Spirit, Alma baptized Helam by God’s authority, as a testimony of his covenant to serve God until death, through Christ’s redemption.

f.w: having authority from the Almighty God

chapters.n: Both Alma and Helam were buried in the water and came up rejoicing and filled with the Spirit. Alma may have been baptizing himself too, as a fresh start.
For the next person, Alma did not immerse himself again.
He baptized everyone who came—about 204 people—who were filled with God’s grace.
They were called the church of God, or church of Christ. All baptized by God’s authority were added to it.
Alma ordained priests—one for every fifty members—to teach the things of God’s kingdom.

f.g: Appointed and given authority by the laying on of hands or other ordinance.

chapters.n: They were to teach only what Alma taught and what the holy prophets had spoken—unlike Noah’s priests.
They were to preach only repentance and faith in the Lord who redeemed his people.

f.w: repentance and faith on the Lord

chapters.n: No contention; one shared vision, one faith, one baptism, hearts “knit together in unity and in love.”
Taught this way, they became the children of God.
Keep the Sabbath holy and give thanks to God every day.
The priests were to support themselves by their own labor—no paid clergy, unlike Noah’s priests.
One day each week they gathered to teach and worship, and also met whenever they could.
Priests received God’s grace instead of pay, growing strong in the Spirit and able to teach with power and authority.
Members were to share according to their means—more from those with more, little from those with little, and help for those with nothing.
This sharing was to be voluntary and from love of God, for priests in need and every needy person.
God commanded this, and the people lived righteously, helping each other spiritually and physically as needed.
A lyrical outburst: the place, waters, and forest of Mormon—how beautiful they are to those who there came to know their Redeemer! They will praise him forever.
All this happened at the land’s border to keep it from the king.
Noah noticed the movement, sent spies, and discovered them as they gathered to hear God’s word.
The king accused Alma of stirring rebellion and sent his army to destroy them.
Warned in time, Alma and the believers packed their tents and families and fled into the wilderness.
By then they numbered about 450 people.
Noah’s army returned after failing to find Alma’s people.
Noah’s forces were weakened, and division grew among the remaining people.
A minority began threatening the king, and serious conflict broke out.
Gideon, a strong man and enemy of the king, drew his sword and swore to kill Noah.

f.g: Later Limhi’s captain; killed by Nehor years afterward (Alma 1:8-9).

chapters.n: As Gideon overpowered him, Noah fled up the tower he had built near the temple.

f.w: the tower which was near the temple

chapters.n: From the top, Noah saw a Lamanite army entering their borders from Shemlon.
He begged Gideon to spare him because the Lamanites were coming to destroy the people.
Noah cared more about saving himself than his people, but Gideon spared him anyway.
Noah ordered everyone to flee into the wilderness with women and children, and he led the way.
The Lamanites caught up and began killing them.
Noah then commanded the men to abandon their wives and children and run—a shocking act of cowardice.
Many men refused and chose to stay and die with their families. The rest abandoned them.
Those who stayed had their daughters step forward to plead with the Lamanites for mercy.
Moved by the women’s beauty, the Lamanites showed compassion.
The Lamanites spared them and let them keep the land on conditions: hand over King Noah and pay half of everything as yearly tribute—fulfilling Abinadi’s warning of bondage.

f.w: one half of all they possessed

chapters.n: Among the captives was Noah’s son Limhi.
Limhi didn’t want his father destroyed, though as a just man he knew his father’s sins.
Gideon secretly sent men to find the king. They met the men who had fled—but not the king and his priests.
These men had resolved to return home and, if their families were dead, take revenge or die with them.
Noah forbade them to return. Angry, they burned him to death—just as Abinadi prophesied.
They were about to kill the priests too, but the priests escaped.
On their way back they met Gideon’s men, who told them their families were alive and under tribute.
The men explained that they had killed the king and the priests had fled deeper into the wilderness.
After a ceremony—perhaps mourning or purification—they returned home rejoicing that their families were alive, and told Gideon what they had done.

f.g: Not explained; possibly a mourning or cleansing rite after Noah’s death.

chapters.n: The Lamanite king swore an oath that his people would not kill them.
The people made Limhi king, and he swore to pay the Lamanite king half of everything.
Limhi began to establish order and peace.
The Lamanite king posted guards around the land—paid from Limhi’s tribute—to keep the people from escaping.
Limhi enjoyed two years of peace without Lamanite attack.
There was a place in Shemlon where young Lamanite women gathered to sing, dance, and celebrate.
One day only a small group gathered there.
Noah’s priests were too ashamed and afraid to return home to their wives and children.
Hiding in the wilderness, they found the Lamanite girls and watched them.
When only a few were present, the priests seized 24 of them and carried them off—a crime that brought war on innocent people. Compare the similar story in Judges 21.
The Lamanites wrongly blamed Limhi’s people.
The Lamanite king led his armies personally to destroy them.
Limhi saw the preparations from the tower and set an ambush in fields and forests.
When the Lamanites arrived, Limhi’s people attacked from hiding.
The fighting was fierce—they fought like lions for prey.
Outnumbered more than two to one, they fought “like dragons” for their lives, wives, and children, and drove the Lamanites back.
They found the Lamanite king wounded among the dead, left behind in his army’s hasty retreat.
They bandaged him, brought him to Limhi, and asked to kill him.
Limhi refused and questioned him: my people kept our oath—why did you break yours?
The king said Limhi’s people had kidnapped Lamanite daughters.
Not knowing of this, Limhi promised to search his people and execute the guilty.
Gideon, now Limhi’s captain, urged him not to blame his own people.
He reasoned: weren’t Noah’s escaped priests in the wilderness? Surely they took the daughters.
Tell the Lamanite king, so he can calm his people—they are preparing to attack again, and we are few.
Unless the king calms his army, they will all die.
Gideon recognizes Abinadi’s prophecies being fulfilled because they ignored the Lord.
Better to stay in bondage than die; let’s keep our oath and stop the bloodshed.
Limhi explained everything about his father and the fugitive priests.
The king was satisfied and swore that his people would not kill Limhi’s people if they came out unarmed.
They followed the king unarmed, and he bowed before his own army and pleaded for Limhi’s people.
Seeing them defenseless, the Lamanites felt compassion and went home peacefully with their king.
After the peace with the Lamanite king, Limhi’s people returned to the city of Nephi and lived peacefully for a time.
After many days the Lamanites grew angry again and began entering the borders of the land.
Bound by their king’s oath, they didn’t kill Limhi’s people, but they struck them, bossed them around, loaded them with heavy burdens, and drove them like donkeys.

f.w: drive them as they would a dumb ass

chapters.n: All this fulfilled the Lord’s word through Abinadi.

f.w: the word of the Lord might be fulfilled

chapters.n: Their suffering was great, and surrounded on all sides, they had no way to free themselves.
The people complained to the king and wanted to fight. Worn down by their complaints, Limhi let them.
They put on armor and went out to drive the Lamanites away.
The Lamanites beat them back and killed many.
There was great mourning—widows for husbands, children for fathers, brothers for brothers.
Many widows cried daily, terrified of the Lamanites.
Their cries angered the remaining men, who fought again and were driven back with heavy losses.
A third attack failed the same way; survivors returned to the city.
At last they humbled themselves “even to the dust,” accepting the yoke of bondage and submitting to their enemies.

f.g: A heavy wooden collar for draft animals; here, slavery.

chapters.n: In deepest humility they cried mightily to God all day for deliverance. Trying their own way first failed; now they turned to God.

Because of their sins, the Lord was slow to answer—as Abinadi warned. Yet he heard them and softened the Lamanites’ hearts to ease their burdens, though he did not free them yet. God often helps step by step.
Gradually they prospered, raising more grain and livestock, so they no longer went hungry.
With many widows, Limhi commanded every man to help support widows and children so none would starve.
They stayed together as much as possible, protecting their grain and flocks.
Limhi never left the city walls without guards, fearing capture.
He had people watch for Noah’s escaped priests, whose kidnapping had caused so much destruction.
The priests had raided the land by night, stealing grain and valuables, so the people lay in wait to punish them.
There were no more Lamanite troubles until Ammon and his brothers arrived.
Limhi, outside the gates, mistook Ammon’s group for Noah’s priests and imprisoned them—he would have executed them had they been the priests.
Learning they were brethren from Zarahemla, he was overjoyed.
Before Ammon came, Limhi had sent men to find Zarahemla, but they got lost.
They found a land of dry bones—a destroyed civilization—thought it was Zarahemla, and came home shortly before Ammon arrived.
They brought back a record engraved on metal plates from those people.
Limhi rejoiced again to learn that King Mosiah could translate such engravings. Ammon rejoiced too.
Yet Ammon’s group grieved for the many who had been killed…
…for the sins Noah and his priests led the people into, for Abinadi’s death, and for Alma’s group, who had formed a church through faith in Abinadi’s words.
They mourned Alma’s departure, not knowing where they went; they would gladly have joined them, having covenanted with God themselves.
Since Ammon’s arrival, Limhi and many of his people had also covenanted to serve God.
They wanted baptism, but no one there had authority from God. Ammon, considering himself unworthy, declined. Priesthood authority matters for ordinances.
So they waited on the Spirit rather than organizing a church, wishing to be like Alma’s people.
They wanted baptism as a witness of wholehearted service, but delayed. Their baptism is described later.
Now everyone’s focus was on escaping Lamanite bondage.
Ammon and Limhi gathered all the people to seek their input on how to escape—an early example of consulting “the voice of the people.”
Fighting was hopeless against so many Lamanites, so the only option was to flee into the wilderness with families, flocks, and tents.
Gideon, Limhi’s trusted captain, comes forward, reminding the king how often he’s listened to his advice.
If he has been a useful servant, Gideon asks to be heard once more—he has a plan to free them.
Limhi lets him speak.
Gideon’s plan: there’s a back pass through the back wall. The Lamanite guards are drunk at night. Gather the flocks to drive them out after dark.
He will deliver the final tribute of wine; when the guards are drunk and asleep, everyone will slip out through the secret pass.

f.g: Part of the payment the Lamanites demanded.

chapters.n: They’ll escape with women, children, flocks, and herds, circling around the land of Shilom.
Limhi agreed to Gideon’s plan.
Limhi gathered the flocks and sent the wine tribute—plus extra wine as a “present.” The guards drank freely.
That night the people left with their flocks, went around Shilom, and headed for Zarahemla, guided by Ammon and his men, who knew the way.
They took all the gold, silver, valuables, and food they could carry.
After many days they reached Zarahemla, joined Mosiah’s people, and became his subjects.
Mosiah welcomed them joyfully and received their records and the gold plates they had found. Those Jaredite plates were later translated into the book of Ether.

f.w: the records which had been found

chapters.n: When the Lamanites discovered the escape, they sent an army after them.
After two days they lost the trail and became lost themselves—setting up the encounter in the next chapter with Alma’s people.

f.w: they were lost in the wilderness

chapters.n: The story returns to Alma. Warned by the Lord that Noah’s army was coming, he and his people gathered their flocks and grain and fled into the wilderness.
The Lord strengthened them so Noah’s army couldn’t catch them.
They traveled eight days into the wilderness.

f.g: A useful clue for Book of Mormon geography: Helam was about eight days from the waters of Mormon.

chapters.n: They found a beautiful, pleasant land with pure water.
They pitched tents, farmed, and built buildings—working very hard.
Because they loved Alma, the people wanted him to be their king.
Alma refuses: the Lord teaches that no one should esteem himself above another, so it isn’t wise to have a king.
If kings could always be just, a king would be good—a point Mosiah II later repeats when ending the monarchy.

f.w: always have just men to be your kings

chapters.n: Remember Noah and his priests! Alma admits he was caught in that trap himself and did terrible things that required painful repentance.
After much struggle, the Lord heard Alma’s prayers and made him an instrument to bring many to the truth. God can use repentant people powerfully.
Still, Alma takes no credit—he is unworthy to boast of himself.
Noah and his priests oppressed them and led them into sin, binding them with the “bands of iniquity.”
Since God freed them from Noah and from sin, they should stand fast in that freedom and trust no man to be king over them.
Trust no one as teacher or minister unless he is a man of God who keeps his commandments.
Alma taught them to love their neighbors as themselves so there would be no contention.
Alma was their high priest, the founder of their church.
No one could preach or teach except by authority from God through Alma. He consecrated only just men as priests and teachers.
These leaders watched over and spiritually nourished the people.
They prospered greatly and named the land Helam—after the first man Alma baptized.
They multiplied and built a city called Helam.
Yet the Lord sometimes disciplines his people, testing their patience and faith. Righteous people still face trials.
But whoever trusts him will be lifted up at the last day—and this people would prove it.

f.w: lifted up at the last day

chapters.n: Mormon previews: they would be enslaved, and only the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob could free them.
God did deliver them with mighty power, and they rejoiced greatly (told in chapter 24).
While farming around Helam, they saw a Lamanite army at their borders—the one that lost Limhi’s trail.
Frightened, they fled their fields and gathered in the city.
Alma stood among them and urged them not to fear but to remember the Lord, who would deliver them.
They quieted their fears and prayed that the Lord would soften the Lamanites’ hearts to spare them and their families.
The Lord softened the Lamanites’ hearts. Alma’s people surrendered, and the Lamanites took over Helam.
This was the Lamanite army that had been lost for many days chasing Limhi’s people.
They had found Noah’s former priests settled in a place called Amulon, farming the land.
The leader of those priests was named Amulon.
Amulon pleaded with the Lamanites and sent his wives—the kidnapped Lamanite daughters—to plead for their husbands’ lives.
For the wives’ sake, the Lamanites spared Amulon and his companions.
Amulon’s group joined the Lamanites. Searching for the land of Nephi, they found Helam.
The Lamanites promised Alma’s people life and freedom if they showed the way to the land of Nephi.
Alma showed them, but the Lamanites broke their promise and set guards over Helam.
Most went on to the land of Nephi; some returned to Helam with the guards’ wives and children.
The Lamanite king made Amulon ruler over Helam—Noah’s former priest now over the very believer he once cast out—though Amulon remained subject to the Lamanite king.

f.w: a king and a ruler over his people

chapters.n: Amulon, the leader of King Noah’s former priests, wins the Lamanite king’s trust. The same men who once lived off Noah’s people now become official teachers across Lamanite lands — a dark irony, since they had abandoned the truth Abinadi taught.
Mormon explains the political setup: the Lamanites now held the former Nephite lands around the city of Nephi, so their high king placed under-kings over each region.

f.w: appointed kings over all these lands
f.g: A layered kingdom — local kings answering to one high king, as later seen with Lamoni and his father.

chapters.n: The Lamanite high king is named Laman, after his father — the same royal name the Lamanites used to honor their ancestor. He ruled a large population.
Amulon’s men spread literacy and the Nephite language through the Lamanite lands. Education itself was a good gift, but as the next verses show, it came without the knowledge of God.

f.g: The written and spoken language of the Nephite records, which Lehi’s family had learned from the brass plates and their fathers.

chapters.n: The Lamanites of this time were kind to one another, yet without God. Amulon’s group taught them nothing of the Lord, the law of Moses, or Abinadi’s words — knowledge they themselves had rejected.
What they did teach was record keeping and letter writing — practical skills that helped commerce and government but left out the sacred purpose for which Nephite records were kept.

With literacy and trade came wealth and worldly cleverness. Mormon notes the Lamanites became shrewd and fond of plunder, though they still dealt fairly with their own people. Learning without God sharpened their skill but not their goodness.

f.g: Clever, crafty — skillful in a self-serving way.

chapters.n: Amulon, now in charge of the land of Helam, begins persecuting Alma’s people and even teaches his own children to bully theirs. Personal grudges shaped his rule.
Amulon’s hatred was personal: Alma had once been a fellow priest of Noah who believed Abinadi and fled. Though Amulon answered to King Laman, he loaded Alma’s people with forced labor and overseers.

f.g: Overseers who drove forced laborers — the same word used of Egypt’s oppression of Israel.

chapters.n: Their suffering grew so heavy that they cried out to God for help, as Israel did in Egypt.
Amulon forbids them even to pray aloud, setting guards and threatening death to anyone caught calling on God. He tried to cut them off from their only real source of help.

f.g: Compare Daniel, who kept praying though a royal decree forbade it.

chapters.n: Unable to pray aloud, they prayed silently in their hearts — and God heard every word. No guard can stop a prayer of the heart.

f.w: he did know the thoughts of their hearts

chapters.n: The Lord answers, telling them to take courage. He remembers the baptismal covenant they made at the waters of Mormon, and promises to keep his side by delivering them.

f.w: the covenant which ye have made unto me

chapters.n: Before taking away their trial, the Lord promises to lighten it so they can hardly feel their burdens. Their experience would make them living witnesses that God visits his people in their suffering.

f.w: visit my people in their afflictions

chapters.n: God kept his word: their loads did not change, but they were strengthened to carry them. They accepted God’s timing cheerfully and patiently — an example of faith while waiting for deliverance.
Because of their faith and patience, the Lord now promises deliverance — and sets the time: tomorrow.
The Lord calls Alma to lead his people out, promising to go with him. Like Moses, Alma leads, but it is God who delivers.
All night the people quietly gather their flocks and grain, preparing to leave — acting on the promise before seeing it fulfilled.

f.g: Compare Israel’s night preparations for the Exodus.

chapters.n: The Lord sends a deep sleep on the Lamanite guards and overseers, so the people can slip away unnoticed. Compare how Limhi’s people escaped by getting their guards drunk; here God himself provides the way.
After a full day’s travel they camp in a valley and name it after Alma, who had led them.

f.g: Naming places after leaders or events is common in the Book of Mormon (compare the land of Helam and the waters of Mormon).

chapters.n: In the valley they pour out thanks to God. They knew clearly that no one but the Lord could have freed them.

f.w: none could deliver them except it were the Lord

chapters.n: Every person old enough to speak joins in praising God — a whole community’s spontaneous worship.

f.w: all their children that could speak
f.g: A detail stressing that the entire community, not just leaders, sang praise.

chapters.n: The Lord warns Alma that the Lamanites have woken and are chasing them. He tells them to hurry on and promises to stop the pursuers in the valley.
Obeying the warning, Alma’s people leave the valley and continue into the wilderness.

f.w: took their journey into the wilderness

chapters.n: After twelve days they reach Zarahemla, where King Mosiah welcomes them joyfully. Both of the groups who had left Zarahemla generations earlier have now returned — Limhi’s people and Alma’s.

f.g: Compare the eight days it took Alma’s group to reach Helam in the first place (Mosiah 23:3).

chapters.n: With both returning groups now safe in Zarahemla, King Mosiah calls the entire population together for a great assembly.
Mormon gives a surprising fact: the descendants of Nephi were a minority in their own land. The people of Zarahemla — descendants of Mulek’s company — outnumbered them.

f.g: A son of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, who escaped Jerusalem’s fall about 587 BC.

chapters.n: Even combined, the Nephites and Mulekites were less than half as many as the Lamanites — a sobering backdrop for the wars that follow in the book of Alma.
The assembly gathers in two groups — Nephites and the people of Zarahemla — showing that the two peoples, though united under one king, still kept distinct identities.
Mosiah reads aloud, and has others read, the record of Zeniff’s colony from the time it left Zarahemla to its return. Much of that record survives in Mosiah 9–22.
He also reads Alma’s account of his group’s journey and sufferings, told in Mosiah 18 and 23–24.
Those who had stayed home in Zarahemla were amazed — for generations they had known little of what happened to Zeniff’s colony.

f.g: Compare the earlier silence: Mosiah 7:1 notes that people in Zarahemla had long wanted to know about those who left.

chapters.n: Seeing the freed people before them filled the listeners with great joy.
But remembering those killed by the Lamanites — including Abinadi and many of Limhi’s men — they wept.
Thinking of God’s quick, recent goodness in freeing Alma’s people, they praised him aloud. The account moves through a range of emotions — joy, grief, gratitude, concern.

f.g: “Immediate” here means direct and present — goodness they could see right before them.

chapters.n: Finally they felt pain for the Lamanites themselves, whom they still called their brethren. Their concern was for the Lamanites’ souls — a feeling that will soon send Mosiah’s sons on their mission.
The children of Amulon’s priests — born to the Lamanite daughters their fathers had kidnapped — reject their fathers’ wicked ways and choose to be called Nephites instead.

f.w: took upon themselves the name of Nephi
f.g: Taking a new name marks a new identity and loyalty — a theme that culminates in taking the name of Christ.

chapters.n: The people of Zarahemla were also counted as Nephites, because the kingship had passed to Nephi’s descendants when Mosiah I arrived and became king over both peoples.

f.w: conferred upon none but those who were descendants of Nephi

chapters.n: After his own reading and speaking, Mosiah invites Alma to address the people — a king making room for a prophet.
Alma goes from group to group, preaching repentance and faith in the Lord — the same simple core message he had taught at the waters of Mormon.

f.w: repentance and faith on the Lord

chapters.n: Alma urges Limhi’s people to remember that their freedom came from the Lord, not merely from their clever escape plan.

f.g: “Remember” is one of the Book of Mormon’s key words; remembering God’s deliverance keeps people humble.
