chapters.n: Limhi and his people now ask for baptism. Earlier they had wanted it but had no one with authority to perform it.

f.w: desirous that he might be baptized

chapters.n: Alma baptizes them in the same way he had at the waters of Mormon, and they become members of the church because they believed his words.

f.w: after the manner he did his brethren in the waters of Mormon

chapters.n: King Mosiah authorizes Alma to establish the church throughout the land and ordain priests and teachers. Civil power supports, but does not run, the church; Alma leads it.
The reason for many congregations was practical: there were too many people for one teacher or one meeting place.

f.w: could not all be governed by one teacher
f.g: Compare Jethro’s counsel to Moses to share the load of leadership.

chapters.n: Each local congregation had its own priests and teachers, and all of them taught what Alma had taught them — keeping the doctrine unified.

f.g: Local congregations, much like wards or branches today.

chapters.n: Though there were many congregations, they formed one church, the church of God, because they taught the same basic message: repentance and faith in God.
There were seven congregations in the land of Zarahemla. Anyone who wanted to take on the name of Christ could join them.

f.w: take upon them the name of Christ

chapters.n: Members were called the people of God. The Lord poured out his Spirit on them, and they prospered — the Book of Mormon’s recurring pattern of blessing for the faithful.
A new problem arises: many young people who were small children at King Benjamin’s great sermon never embraced their parents’ faith. Each generation must gain its own conviction.

f.g: The young people growing up; compare Judges 2:10, where a new generation “knew not the Lord.”

chapters.n: Their unbelief centered on two core teachings: that the dead will rise, and that Christ would come.
Mormon makes a key point: their unbelief came first, and it kept them from understanding. Spiritual things are understood through faith, and a hardened heart shuts them out.

f.w: could not understand the word of God

chapters.n: They refused baptism and church membership, staying a separate group in belief. “Carnal” means focused on bodily, worldly desires rather than spiritual ones.

f.g: Fleshly; governed by physical appetites and worldly concerns.

chapters.n: At first they were less than half as many as the believers, but quarrels within the church helped them grow.

f.g: Disagreements that split a group apart.

chapters.n: Using flattery, they led many church members into sin. So the church needed a way to correct members who sinned — the first church discipline in the Nephite record.
Offenders were brought by teachers to priests, and by priests to Alma, the presiding high priest — a simple chain of local leadership.
Mormon clarifies that Mosiah had given Alma authority over the church, so church matters were Alma’s to handle.
Alma had no personal knowledge of these cases, but many witnesses came forward and testified about the wrongdoing.
This was the church’s first case of this kind, so Alma felt troubled and unsure. He brought the offenders to the king, assuming it was a civil matter.

f.g: Deeply worried — Alma was anxious to handle the matter rightly.

chapters.n: Alma explains to Mosiah that these people are accused by fellow members, have been caught in various sins, and are not repentant. He asks the king to judge them.
Mosiah declines: these are church matters, and he hands them back to Alma. The king keeps civil and religious authority distinct.

f.g: Sins against the church, not crimes against the law, belonged to church leaders to judge.

chapters.n: Troubled again, Alma turns to the Lord in prayer because he fears acting wrongly before God. A wise leader asks before he acts.
After Alma pours out his whole soul in prayer, the Lord answers him directly.
The Lord first blesses Alma for believing Abinadi’s words alone — without signs or proof — and blesses those he baptized at Mormon.

f.w: the words alone of my servant Abinadi

chapters.n: Likewise, Alma’s converts are blessed because they believed his words alone. Faith passed along by testimony is precious to the Lord.
The Lord blesses Alma for founding the church and promises that its members will be established as the Lord’s own people.
Those willing to carry the Lord’s name belong to him. Taking his name means a relationship of ownership and love: “they are mine.”
The Lord blesses Alma simply for asking what to do. Seeking God’s will before acting is itself righteous.
An extraordinary promise: the Lord covenants that Alma will have eternal life, and calls him to gather the Lord’s sheep.

f.g: Compare similar sure promises in D&C 132:49 and Enos 1:27.

chapters.n: The Lord’s sheep are those who hear his voice. Whoever the church receives on those terms, the Lord receives too.
This is the Lord’s church, not Alma’s. Baptism is “unto repentance,” and those who believe in Christ’s name receive his free forgiveness.
Christ explains why he can forgive: he takes on himself the world’s sins and he created all people. Those who keep believing to the end receive a place at his right hand.

f.w: taketh upon me the sins of the world

chapters.n: Those called by his name who truly know him will rise to an eternal place at his right hand — the place of honor and salvation.

f.g: The place of favor and covenant blessing; compare the sheep on the right in the Savior’s parable.

chapters.n: At the “second trump,” those who never knew the Lord will rise and stand before him at the judgment.

f.g: Trumpet calls mark stages of the resurrection; later revelation describes a sequence of trumps.

chapters.n: Then they will recognize him as their Lord and Redeemer — but too late, because they refused his redemption.
The Lord will declare he never knew them, and they will be sent away — echoing the Savior’s own words in the New Testament.

f.g: Scripture’s image for the anguish of being cut off from God.

chapters.n: So the rule for church membership is clear: those who will not hear the Lord’s voice should not be received, since he will not receive them at the last day.
The Lord gives Alma the principle: judge transgressors by their sins, but forgive those who sincerely confess and repent, as God himself will forgive.
A tender promise: every time the Lord’s people repent, he will forgive them. His mercy is not used up.

f.w: as often as my people repent

chapters.n: Members must forgive one another too. Refusing to forgive someone who says they repent puts the unforgiving person under condemnation.
The Lord closes: those who will not repent cannot be counted among his people, and this rule stands from now on.

f.w: shall not be numbered among my people

chapters.n: Alma writes the revelation down so he can follow it exactly in judging church members — a model for recording revelation.
Alma then judges the accused according to the Lord’s word.

f.w: according to the word of the Lord
f.g: Alma acts on revealed guidance rather than his own feelings.

chapters.n: Those who repented and confessed stayed in the church.

f.w: repented of their sins and did confess them

chapters.n: Those who refused were removed from church records — their names “blotted out.” This was church discipline, not civil punishment.
With order restored, the church enjoyed peace and growth. Members walked “circumspectly” — carefully, watching their steps — and many were baptized.
Alma and his fellow leaders worked hard, taught faithfully, and endured persecution from those outside the church.
Leaders corrected others and were corrected themselves — no one was above the word of God. All were commanded to pray always and give thanks in everything.
Unbelievers’ persecution of the church grows so severe that members complain to Alma, who takes the matter to King Mosiah. Mosiah consults his priests before acting.
Mosiah issues a royal decree across the land: no unbeliever may persecute church members. Religious freedom is protected by law.

f.g: An official public announcement from the king.

chapters.n: The church also commands its own members not to persecute anyone, and to treat all people as equals — the protection works both ways.
Members must not let pride disturb their peace, should value their neighbors as themselves, and should support themselves by their own work.
Even priests and teachers were to support themselves by their own labor, except when sick or in great need. There was no paid clergy — and the church abounded in God’s grace.
Peace returns, and the population grows and spreads in every direction, building cities and villages throughout the land.

f.g: Mormon often frames Nephite geography by compass directions from Zarahemla.

chapters.n: The Lord blesses them, and they become large and wealthy — a prosperity that, as later chapters show, can become its own test.
Shockingly, the king’s own sons and the high priest’s son, Alma the Younger, are among the unbelievers. Young Alma is a persuasive, flattering speaker who leads many people astray.

f.g: Worshiping idols — or, more broadly, putting anything in God’s place.

chapters.n: Alma the Younger becomes a serious obstacle to the church, stealing people’s loyalty and stirring up division, which gave Satan more power over them.

f.w: stealing away the hearts of the people
f.g: An echo of Absalom, who “stole the hearts” of Israel from his father David.

chapters.n: Alma and Mosiah’s sons work secretly to destroy the church — defying God and even breaking the king’s own decree.

f.g: Compare Saul of Tarsus, who also set out to destroy the church before his conversion.

chapters.n: As they go about their rebellion, an angel descends in a cloud, speaking with a voice like thunder that shakes the ground beneath them.

f.w: the angel of the Lord appeared unto them

chapters.n: Overwhelmed, they fall to the ground and cannot at first understand what the angel says.
The angel calls Alma by name and asks why he persecutes God’s church. The Lord promises his church will stand; only his own people’s sins can overthrow it.

f.w: why persecutest thou the church of God
save it is the transgression of my people
f.g: No outside enemy can destroy the church; the real danger comes from within.

chapters.n: The angel explains why he has come: God has heard the faithful prayers of the church and especially of Alma’s father for his son. This visit answers a parent’s prayers.

f.w: he has prayed with much faith concerning thee

chapters.n: With the ground still shaking, the angel challenges them: can you deny God’s power now? You can see me, and I am sent by God.

f.w: can ye dispute the power of God

chapters.n: The angel tells Alma to remember how God freed his father’s people from bondage in Helam and Nephi, and to stop fighting the church — even if he himself chose to be lost.

f.w: if thou wilt of thyself be cast off
f.g: Alma’s agency is respected: he can still choose his own path, but must stop harming others.

chapters.n: The angel finishes speaking and leaves.

f.g: The whole visit was brief — but it changed the course of Nephite history.

chapters.n: They fall to the earth again. They had seen an angel with their own eyes and knew only God’s power could shake the earth like that.
Alma is struck speechless and too weak to move, so his companions carry him helpless to his father. His account in Alma 36 says this lasted three days and nights.
His companions tell his father everything, and the elder Alma rejoices, recognizing God’s power at work in his son.
Alma’s father gathers a crowd so they can witness what God has done for his son and companions.

f.g: The miracle became a public testimony, not a private family matter.

chapters.n: The priests fast and pray that young Alma might regain his speech and strength, so that the people might see God’s goodness and glory.
After two days and nights of fasting and prayer, Alma recovers, stands, and tells the people to take comfort.

f.g: Alma 36:10 says he lay unable to move three days and three nights in all.

chapters.n: His first words are a testimony: he has repented, been redeemed by the Lord, and been born of the Spirit.
Alma relays what the Lord taught him: every person, of every nation and people, must be born again — changed from a fallen state to righteousness, becoming God’s sons and daughters.
Being born again makes people “new creatures.” Without this inner change, no one can inherit God’s kingdom.
Those not reborn will be cast off — and Alma knows this personally because he nearly was.

f.w: I was like to be cast off
f.g: “Like to be” = on the verge of being.

chapters.n: After passing through great suffering and repenting almost to the point of death, the Lord mercifully rescued him from an “everlasting burning.”

f.w: snatch me out of an everlasting burning

chapters.n: Alma uses vivid contrasts: bitterness and chains, then freedom; a dark pit, then God’s marvelous light; torment, then peace. Alma 36 tells this experience in fuller detail.

f.g: Gall was an intensely bitter substance; the phrase means deep, poisonous misery.

chapters.n: Alma confesses he had rejected the Redeemer and denied the prophecies. Now he testifies that Christ will come and make himself known to all he created.

f.w: he remembereth every creature of his creating

chapters.n: Quoting Isaiah’s image, Alma testifies that all will one day bow and confess Christ as God. The ungodly will then admit their judgment is just and shrink before his all-seeing eye.

f.w: every knee shall bow, and every tongue confess

chapters.n: From then on Alma and his companions travel throughout the land, telling everyone what they had seen and heard, while enduring persecution and even beatings.
Despite opposition, they comfort and strengthen the church, patiently urging members to keep God’s commandments.
Four of Alma’s companions were the king’s sons: Ammon, Aaron, Omner, and Himni — names that will fill the coming chapters of Alma.

f.w: Ammon, and Aaron, and Omner, and Himni

chapters.n: They travel through Mosiah’s kingdom trying to undo the harm they had caused, openly confessing their sins and teaching the scriptures. Real repentance includes making restitution where possible.

f.g: Restitution — making right what one has damaged — is part of true repentance.

chapters.n: They became God’s instruments in bringing many people to know the truth and their Redeemer.

f.w: instruments in the hands of God

chapters.n: Mormon exclaims how blessed they are, borrowing Isaiah’s words about messengers who publish peace and good tidings and announce that the Lord reigns.

Having worked to repair the damage they had done at home, Mosiah’s sons, with a few chosen companions, ask their father’s permission to go preach to the Lamanites in the land of Nephi — the very people Nephites feared most.

f.w: go up to the land of Nephi
f.g: “Up” because the land of Nephi lay at a higher elevation than Zarahemla.

chapters.n: Their hopes are bold: to bring the Lamanites to God, to correct false traditions, to heal centuries of hatred, and to end the fighting between the two peoples.
Having felt the terror of their own near-loss, they cannot bear the thought of any soul suffering endless torment. Their own conversion produced deep love for others.

f.w: they could not bear that any human soul should perish

chapters.n: Mormon calls them “the very vilest of sinners,” yet God mercifully spared them. They still suffered intense anguish and feared being cast off forever — repentance was real and painful.
They plead with their father for many days to let them go.

f.g: Earnestly ask; Mosiah had good reason to fear for their lives.

chapters.n: Wisely, Mosiah asks the Lord whether to let his sons go.
The Lord answers with three promises: many Lamanites will believe, the believers will gain eternal life, and Mosiah’s sons will be protected.
Mosiah grants their request — a father trusting God with his sons’ lives.
The sons set out into the wilderness. Mormon promises to tell their story later — which he does in Alma 17–26.

f.w: I shall give an account of their proceedings hereafter

chapters.n: This creates a problem: none of Mosiah’s sons wants the throne, so he has no heir.

f.w: not any of his sons who would accept of the kingdom

chapters.n: Before handing over the sacred records, Mosiah finishes translating the 24 gold plates that Limhi’s explorers had found — the record of the Jaredites.

f.w: plates of gold which had been found by the people of Limhi

chapters.n: He did this because his people were extremely eager to learn about the destroyed nation whose ruins and bones had been found.

f.w: those people who had been destroyed

chapters.n: Mosiah translated using two stones fastened in the rims of a bow — what Latter-day Saints call the interpreters, or Urim and Thummim.

f.w: two stones which were fastened into the two rims of a bow
f.g: Joseph Smith described receiving a similar instrument with the gold plates.

chapters.n: These interpreters had been prepared long ago and passed down through generations specifically to translate languages.
The Lord preserved them so that the sins and fate of past peoples could be revealed to later inhabitants of the land — a warning from history.
Whoever possesses these instruments is called a “seer,” an old title for one who sees what others cannot.
The Jaredite record reached back from their destruction to the Tower of Babel, and even further to the creation of Adam. The Book of Ether is Moroni’s abridgment of it.
The story of a whole civilization’s destruction saddened the people, yet they rejoiced in the knowledge it gave them.
Mormon notes this account will be written later because everyone should know it — fulfilled when Moroni included the Book of Ether.

f.w: this account shall be written hereafter

chapters.n: Mosiah transfers all the sacred records and the interpreters to Alma the Younger, commanding him to keep them and continue the history — a chain stretching back to Lehi.

f.w: handing them down from one generation to another

chapters.n: With no willing heir, Mosiah does something unusual for a king: he asks the people who they want as their next ruler.

f.g: Consulting the people foreshadows the government by “the voice of the people” he is about to propose.

chapters.n: The people choose Aaron, one of Mosiah’s sons.
But Aaron has already left for the land of Nephi, and none of Mosiah’s sons wants the throne. Their mission mattered more to them than a crown.

f.w: neither would Aaron take upon him the kingdom

chapters.n: So Mosiah sends a written proclamation among the people. What follows (verses 5–32) is his letter proposing a new form of government.

f.g: Putting it in writing let every community read and weigh the same argument.

chapters.n: Mosiah addresses the people as brothers, not just subjects, and asks them to think carefully about their wish for a king.
He reminds them that the rightful heir has declined the throne.

f.w: he to whom the kingdom doth rightly belong
f.g: Likely Aaron, whom the people had named in verse 2.

chapters.n: Mosiah worries that appointing someone else could backfire: the rightful heir might later change his mind, gather followers, and start a civil war — as Amlici later tries to do anyway.

f.w: draw away a part of this people after him

chapters.n: He urges wisdom: they have no right to harm his son, nor any substitute king. A succession fight would hurt everyone.

f.g: Mosiah reasons with his people rather than simply commanding them.

chapters.n: If Aaron ever fell back into pride, he might reclaim the throne, leading both himself and the people into sin.
Mosiah asks them to look ahead and choose whatever will keep the peace.
His plan: he will remain king for life, but the nation will shift to elected judges who will judge by the law and God’s commandments.

f.g: The start of the “reign of the judges,” which became the Nephite calendar from Alma 1 onward.

chapters.n: Mosiah states a principle: God’s judgments are always just, but human judgments are not. So a system should guard against human failure.

f.w: the judgments of God are always just

chapters.n: If kings could always be as righteous as his father Benjamin, monarchy would be best. But that cannot be guaranteed.
Mosiah describes his own reign: he worked with all his strength to teach God’s commandments and keep peace, free of war, theft, and murder.

f.w: labored with all the power and faculties

chapters.n: He punished wrongdoing only according to the law handed down from their fathers — not by personal whim.
Because not all people are just, it is unwise to entrust power to a king.
One wicked king can cause enormous sin and destruction among his people.
Mosiah points to a recent example everyone just heard about: King Noah, whose wickedness led his people into destruction and bondage.
Only God’s intervention, prompted by their sincere repentance, freed Noah’s people.
God freed them because they humbled themselves and cried to him. Mosiah draws a broad lesson: the Lord extends mercy to all who trust him.
A practical problem with kings: removing a wicked one usually requires conflict and bloodshed.
A wicked king surrounds himself with corrupt friends and guards, tears up the righteous laws of his predecessors, and tramples God’s commandments.
He makes laws that suit his wickedness and destroys anyone who resists. In this way an unrighteous king corrupts a whole nation’s sense of right.

f.g: Twist away from what is right.

chapters.n: Mosiah does not want his people to suffer such evils.
So he proposes that the people choose judges by their own voice, to judge by laws given through their fathers by the Lord.

f.w: by the voice of this people

chapters.n: A key principle: the majority usually chooses right, while a smaller part often wants wrong. So decisions should be made by “the voice of the people.”

f.g: Not pure democracy in the modern sense, but a system of chosen judges accountable to the people.

chapters.n: A sober warning: when the majority chooses evil, God’s judgments will follow. This prophecy is fulfilled later in Nephite history.

f.w: the voice of the people doth choose iniquity

chapters.n: Checks and balances: a judge who breaks the law can be judged by a higher judge.
And if higher judges go wrong, a group of lower judges can judge them — no one stands above the law.
Mosiah commands these changes and that they have no king, so each person will be responsible for his own sins rather than being led into them by a ruler.
Many peoples sin because their kings lead them astray, so that guilt rests on the kings.
Mosiah’s great hope: no more inequality, but a land of liberty where everyone enjoys the same rights — a vision that resonates with later ideals of freedom.
Mosiah wrote much more, describing the burdens of a righteous king — his anxieties for the people and the complaints he received.
He taught that the burden of government should not rest on one man; every person should share responsibility.

f.w: every man might bear his part

chapters.n: He also explained the many disadvantages of living under an unrighteous king.
He listed the evils such kings bring — wars, bloodshed, theft, sexual sin, and more — all contrary to God’s commandments.
Persuaded by his reasoning, the people accepted his words.

f.w: convinced of the truth of his words
f.g: The change came by persuasion, not force.

chapters.n: They gave up wanting a king and became eager for everyone to have an equal chance, each willing to answer for his own sins.
The people gathered across the land to vote for judges, rejoicing in their new freedom.
Their love for Mosiah grew. He had never sought wealth, never enjoyed bloodshed, and had freed them from bondage — so they honored him above any other man.

f.g: Money or profit, especially gained dishonestly.
A cruel ruler with absolute power.

chapters.n: Judges were appointed throughout the land to govern according to the law.

f.g: Compare the judges Moses appointed in Israel.

chapters.n: Alma the Younger becomes the first chief judge while also serving as high priest over the church, having received that charge from his father.
Alma governs righteously and the land enjoys continual peace — at least for now.
So begins the reign of the judges over the Nephites — about 91 BC. The book of Alma will count years from this point.
Alma the Elder dies at eighty-two, having faithfully kept God’s commandments.

f.g: He was born about 173 BC, according to this reckoning.

chapters.n: Mosiah also dies at sixty-three, after thirty-three years as king — 509 years after Lehi left Jerusalem.

f.g: Counting from 600 BC, this is about 91 BC.

chapters.n: Thus ends the line of Nephite kings, and the life of Alma, founder of the church among this people. A new era begins.
